issues.legal_issue: A management-takeover order based on an investigation and serious deterioration in an undertaking’s affairs is not invalidated merely because the government also supported the undertaking financially.
material_facts: An investigation found that the undertaking was being managed in a manner highly detrimental to public interest.
The undertaking had run at a loss and had closed before the takeover order was made.
The state government had sanctioned a guarantee to help the company raise a loan, following consideration of the investigation committee’s recommendations.
The undertaking was later included in the legislation’s schedule as a sick textile undertaking.
issues.conclusion: The takeover order had a sufficient basis, and the financial assistance did not establish that the order was unfounded or illegal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the investigation and the government’s resulting finding under section 18A(b) of the Industrial (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951, that management was highly detrimental to public interest. The undertaking’s losses and closure supported that finding; the separate decision to assist it financially did not negate the investigation. The Court also stated that a legislative judgment identifying an undertaking as sick should be respected and requires very strong grounds to set aside.

rule.if: management_takeover_challenged and investigation_found_public_harm and undertaking_was_financially_distressed and financial_assistance_was_granted and no_strong_basis_to_reject_sick_classification

predicates.management_takeover_challenged: The affected party challenged an order taking over the management of an industrial undertaking.
predicates.investigation_found_public_harm: An investigation found that the undertaking was managed in a way highly detrimental to the public interest.
predicates.undertaking_was_financially_distressed: The undertaking was running at a loss or had ceased operating.
predicates.financial_assistance_was_granted: The government supported the undertaking financially or helped it obtain financing.
predicates.no_strong_basis_to_reject_sick_classific: No strong ground was established for rejecting the legislative classification of the undertaking as sick.

issues.definition: When a challenged management takeover follows an investigation finding public harm in a financially distressed undertaking, the fact that financial assistance was granted does not defeat the order’s sufficient basis where no strong ground undermines the sick classification.

issues.legal_issue: A prior direction to an industrial undertaking is not a prerequisite to taking over its management when the takeover is based on an investigation finding management highly detrimental to public interest.
material_facts: The undertaking’s management was taken over after an investigation under section 15 of the Industrial (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951.
The takeover was based on the finding that the undertaking was being managed in a manner highly detrimental to public interest.
The government had not issued a direction under section 16 of that Act.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a prior direction did not invalidate the takeover order.
issues.legal_principle: Section 18A provided distinct grounds for taking over management: failure to comply with directions, and management highly detrimental to the scheduled industry or public interest after an investigation, whether or not directions had been issued. The Court held that issuing directions under section 16 was not obligatory in every case.

rule.if: management_takeover_challenged and investigation_was_conducted and investigation_found_public_harm and no_prior_corrective_direction

predicates.management_takeover_challenged: The affected party challenged an order taking over the management of an industrial undertaking.
predicates.investigation_was_conducted: The government conducted an investigation into the undertaking’s affairs before taking over its management.
predicates.investigation_found_public_harm: The investigation led to a finding that the undertaking was managed in a way highly detrimental to the public interest or the relevant industry.
predicates.no_prior_corrective_direction: The government had not first issued a direction requiring the undertaking to correct its conduct.

issues.definition: If a management takeover follows an investigation finding serious public harm, the absence of an earlier corrective direction does not invalidate the takeover.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to supply an investigation report does not, by itself, establish a denial of natural justice when the affected party had a fair opportunity to be heard and suffered no prejudice.
material_facts: The company was given a hearing by the investigation committee and an opportunity to make representations against the proposed takeover.
The company was not supplied with a copy of the investigation report and had not asked for one.
The Court found that the petitioners were not prejudiced by the report’s non-supply.
issues.conclusion: Non-supply of the report did not invalidate the takeover order in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Whether non-supply of an investigation report breaches natural justice depends on the facts and circumstances, including whether it prevented an effective representation. Applying Keshav Mills Co. Ltd. v. Union of India, the Court held that a party given fair treatment and reasonable opportunities to present its case could not establish a breach merely because it was not given the report; prejudice was absent here.

rule.if: management_takeover_challenged and investigation_report_not_supplied and affected_party_received_a_fair_hearing and no_material_prejudice_from_non_supply

predicates.management_takeover_challenged: The affected party challenged an order taking over the management of an industrial undertaking.
predicates.investigation_report_not_supplied: The government did not provide the affected party with the report of the investigation preceding the takeover.
predicates.affected_party_received_a_fair_hearing: The affected party had a reasonable opportunity to be heard and to make representations about the proposed action.
predicates.no_material_prejudice_from_non_supply: The affected party was not materially prevented from making an effective representation by not receiving the report.

issues.definition: When a party challenging a management takeover had a fair hearing and was not materially prejudiced, the report’s non-supply does not invalidate the takeover.

issues.legal_issue: A delayed challenge to a management-takeover order may be rejected where the affected parties did not challenge it before nationalisation and the circumstances show that they were not aggrieved by it.
material_facts: The petitioners did not challenge the takeover order before the undertaking was nationalised, although several years had passed since the order.
They did not ask for a copy of the investigation report.
The company lacked the resources considered necessary to run the mill, and the Court concluded that the petitioners were not aggrieved by the takeover order.
The petitioners later challenged the order in court after nationalisation.
issues.conclusion: In view of these circumstances, the petitioners were not entitled to challenge the takeover order.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the lapse of several years, the failure to challenge the order before nationalisation, the failure to request the report, and the company’s lack of resources to operate the mill. It treated these circumstances as grounds for not permitting the challenge, apart from its determination of the substantive objections to the order.

predicates.management_takeover_challenged: The affected party challenged an order taking over the management of an industrial undertaking.
predicates.challenge_was_delayed_until_after_nation: The challenge was brought only after the undertaking had been nationalised, several years after the management-takeover order.
predicates.no_earlier_challenge_was_made: The affected party did not contest the takeover order before nationalisation.
predicates.affected_party_lacked_capacity_to_run_th: The affected party lacked the resources needed to operate the undertaking.

issues.definition: A challenge brought only after nationalisation may not be entertained when the affected party did not contest the earlier takeover and lacked the capacity to run the undertaking.

issues.legal_issue: Legislation that gives effect to the policy of distributing community resources for the common good cannot be challenged on the ground that it violates equality or freedom of trade where the applicable constitutional protection covers it.
material_facts: The Nationalisation Act was enacted to reorganise and rehabilitate sick textile undertakings and to promote production and distribution for the public good.
The Act declared that it gave effect to the policy of the State towards the principles concerning community resources and the common good.
The petitioners did not contend that the Act failed to give effect to that policy.
issues.conclusion: The petitioners could not challenge the Act on the ground that it violated Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the Act gave effect to the policy reflected in Article 39(b), concerning ownership and control of material resources and their distribution to best serve the common good. Because the Act was protected by Article 31C, the petitioners could not challenge it for violating Articles 14 and 19. The Court relied on the protection of Article 31C as upheld in Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala and discussed in Waman Rao v. Union of India.

predicates.constitutional_validity_of_public_resour: A party challenged the constitutional validity of a law reorganising or nationalising an undertaking.
predicates.law_advances_common_good_distribution_of: The law gives effect to a policy of organising ownership or control of community resources so their distribution serves the common good.
predicates.policy_basis_is_not_disputed: The challenger did not establish that the law failed to give effect to the policy it declared.
predicates.constitutional_protection_for_that_polic: The constitutional protection for laws implementing that policy applies to the law.

issues.definition: When a challenged reorganisation law implements an undisputed policy of distributing community resources for the common good and the applicable constitutional protection covers it, an equality or trade-freedom challenge is barred.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge that a statute damages the Constitution’s basic structure must be directed to a constitutional amendment that placed it in the protected schedule, and the challenge is otiose if the statute is independently protected by the applicable constitutional saving.
material_facts: The Nationalisation Act had been included in the Ninth Schedule by a constitutional amendment made after the date identified in Waman Rao.
The petitioners argued that the Act damaged basic or essential features of the Constitution as reflected in Articles 14 and 19.
The Court found that the Act was protected by Article 31C as it stood before the Forty-Second Amendment.
issues.conclusion: The basic-structure challenge did not permit the petitioners to challenge the Act under Articles 14 and 19 because the Act was protected by the applicable pre-amendment constitutional saving.
issues.legal_principle: Relying on Waman Rao v. Union of India and Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, the Court stated that post-April 24, 1973 constitutional amendments placing legislation in the Ninth Schedule may be challenged for damaging the basic structure. But where the legislation is saved by Article 31A or Article 31C as it stood before the Forty-Second Amendment, such a challenge to the schedule-inserting amendment, insofar as it rests on Articles 14 or 19, becomes otiose. The Court also stated that damage to the basic structure is attributed to constitutional amendments, not to ordinary statutes as such.

predicates.basic_structure_challenge_to_scheduled_l: A party argued that a law included in a constitutionally protected schedule damages an essential feature or basic structure of the Constitution.
predicates.schedule_insertion_was_by_later_constitu: The law was placed in the schedule by a constitutional amendment made after the relevant constitutional cutoff.
predicates.law_is_independently_covered_by_an_exist: The law is protected by a constitutional saving that existed before the later amendment.

issues.definition: A basic-structure challenge concerning a scheduled law is otiose when the law is independently protected by an existing constitutional saving, even if its schedule inclusion resulted from a later constitutional amendment.

issues.legal_issue: Vacant land within an undertaking’s compound and in the owner’s possession, power, or control forms part of the undertaking even if it has not been used for the undertaking.
material_facts: The disputed vacant land lay within the mill compound and was in the company’s ownership, possession, power, or control.
The petitioners argued that the land was unrelated to the undertaking and that it had not been used since the management takeover.
The Nationalisation Act defined the sick textile undertaking to include the owner’s movable and immovable properties, including land.
issues.conclusion: The whole of the disputed vacant land formed part of the textile undertaking and did not have to be returned to the company.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 4(1) of the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 1974, a sick textile undertaking includes property, including land, in the ownership, possession, power, or control of its owner. Whether vacant land was actually used is not relevant to that inclusion. The Court distinguished National Textile Corporation Ltd. v. Sitaram Mills Ltd., explaining that it did not establish that land must be used to be an asset of the undertaking.

rule.if: nationalisation_property_dispute and land_is_within_the_undertaking_compound and land_is_owned_or_controlled_by_the_undertaking_owner and land_is_unused

predicates.nationalisation_property_dispute: A party disputed whether property vested as part of a nationalised undertaking.
predicates.land_is_within_the_undertaking_compound: The disputed land lies within the undertaking’s compound.
predicates.land_is_owned_or_controlled_by_the_under: The land is owned, possessed, or controlled by the owner of the undertaking.
predicates.land_is_unused: The disputed land is vacant or has not been used for the undertaking.

issues.definition: In a nationalisation property dispute, unused land within the undertaking’s compound and owned or controlled by its owner forms part of the undertaking.
